entries.title: What Design Can't Do: Essays on Design and Disillusion — Prologue
entries.author: Silvio Lorusso
entries.note: Lorusso opens by admitting design can't actually fix the disorder it claims to manage — it can only rearrange it, or dress it up as order. That's exactly the tension in my 'Order to Mess / Chaos' and 'Chaos & Order' concepts for 256: a grid doesn't remove the mess underneath it, it just gives a frame to look at the mess through. Reading the Prologue made me want to stop treating 'ordered' and 'chaotic' as opposite states to pick between, and start treating order as a lens I place over chaos on purpose — sometimes tight, sometimes barely holding. It's already changing how I'm picking images: I'm pulling ones where you can feel the underlying disorder pushing against whatever structure contains it, not ones that are just clean or just messy on their own.

09/02 Restrictions / Contraints
https://www.play.teaching-documents.org/restrictions-mevis-van-deursen/

- restrictions that are more aligned tend to be more intersting to push towards
- exclusively do what you enjoy doing and try pushing it more

generative restrictions - explore
try restrictions and try them out - dont have to justify
how do you choose restriction?

- intensify - more myself
- reduce / go against the grain - challenge myself to try something new
- reverse engineering
- tree search and then narrow down
- After thinking and discussing
- Intensify — exaggerate something already present in your practice to make the work feel more like you.
- Reduce — remove something you typically depend on, such as color, imagery, scale, or animation.
- Go against the grain — deliberately work in a style or process that feels unfamiliar.
- Reverse-engineer — begin with a desired outcome and work backward to determine the necessary rules.
- Tree search — explore many possible directions, then progressively eliminate options.
- Randomize — allow chance to determine certain choices, such as color, typeface, order, or composition.
- Repeat — use one element, gesture, shape, or system throughout the entire project.
- Transform — begin with one source and establish rules for repeatedly altering it.
- Translate — move something from one medium, sensory form, or visual language into another.
- Substitute — replace a familiar tool, material, or element with an unexpected alternative.
- Invert — reverse the usual hierarchy, reading order, scale, function, or relationship.
- Misuse — use a tool or material for something it was not designed to do.
- Respond to the material — allow the properties of the medium to determine the outcome.
- Respond to the site — derive restrictions from the physical or social context in which the work appears.
- Respond to the audience — base the rules on how a specific person or community might encounter the work.
- Time-box — limit how long you can ideate, produce, revise, or make each decision.
- Quantity-limit — restrict the number of colors, typefaces, images, words, shapes, frames, or interactions.
- Scale-limit — work only at an unusually small, large, or fixed size.
- Tool-limit — complete the project using only one tool, program, technique, or machine.
- Source-limit — construct everything from one image, text, archive, object, or dataset.
- Rule-based generation — create a fixed set of instructions that produces the design.
- Conditional logic — use "if–then" rules so the design changes in response to specific conditions.
- Sequential constraint — allow each decision to depend entirely on the one made before it.
- Preserve and intervene — keep most of an existing object or system unchanged and alter only one part.
- Design for failure — introduce a rule that allows errors, breakdowns, or imperfections to shape the outcome.
- Set a contradiction — require the work to satisfy two seemingly opposing qualities, such as loud and minimal or rigid and playful.
- Borrow a system — apply rules from music, games, coding, architecture, or another discipline.
- Let content lead — derive every visual decision directly from the meaning or structure of the content.
- Let form lead — begin with a formal rule and discover what content it can produce.
- Physicalize — require every element to be made or tested physically before becoming digital.
- One-variable exploration — keep everything constant except one element, then examine how changing it affects the work.

- Grid Meaning (256 Part 2 ideation process)
  - Grids that contain
  - Grids that separate
  - Grids that guide
  - Grids that measure
  - Grids that repeat
  - Grids that control
  - Grids that decorate
  - Grids that break

The website could initially present one perfect grid. When someone selects a meaning, the images reorganize according to it. The actual grid system could also change:
- "Organize" creates an orderly modular layout.
- "Separate" introduces large gaps and visible borders.
- "Control" locks every image into identical cells.
- "Repeat" duplicates images and patterns.
- "Play" changes color, scale, and placement.
- "Break" allows images to overlap and escape their cells.

References pulled from this: Prisma Tent (Lineto), Irma Boom, Motionographer, SiteInspire, The Medium is the Message, Blurb, Newspaper Club — see the linked entries under #256-part-2.
